In the village akhada near Rohtak, Coach Yogesh noticed Swati was always first on the mat now, before sunrise, and last to leave after dark. Since her engagement was broken off in spring, she hadn't missed a single session. She threw partners harder than before, did extra rope climbs, and snapped at anyone who suggested a rest day. Yogesh watched her grip the rope until her palms blistered.
One evening he sat beside her at the edge of the mat. "Your training is fire, Swati. I'm glad it's here and not somewhere worse. But fire needs fuel. Tomorrow you rest. And if you ever want to talk about what's behind all this, I can listen, or I'll find you someone better at it than me."
Swati stared at her taped hands for a long time. Then she nodded.

qa.q: What happened to Swati's palms from gripping the rope?
qa.a: They blistered.

qa.q: Why might training harder feel right to Swati since spring?
qa.a: Throwing her anger and hurt onto the mat gives them a safe, useful outlet, so she doesn't have to face them directly.

qa.q: What choice did Yogesh make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: He praised the channel but insisted on a rest day and offered someone to talk to, because training alone can't carry what's underneath.

qa.q: How might Swati's training partners feel about being thrown harder?
qa.a: They may feel bruised and wary, noticing her anger even if they don't know the reason.

grounding: A wrestling coach sees a young woman pour anger into relentless training and tells her the channel stays healthy only with rest and someone to talk to.

Marek had coached the rugby club in Wrocław for twenty years, and he recognised the look. Since Bilal's father left the family in autumn, the young flanker had been furious in every direction: slamming lockers, arguing with referees. Then something shifted. Bilal started coming to the gym at six every morning, running hill sprints alone, staying after practice to hit the tackling bag. His anger had found a job.
Marek was glad. But he also noticed Bilal limping, skipping meals, and changing the subject whenever anyone mentioned home. After Thursday's session, Marek handed him a water bottle. "You're training like a man possessed. That's useful, up to a point. You also need sleep, and someone to talk to about your dad. The club counsellor is good. Or I'm here."
Bilal looked at the grass. "Maybe," he said.

qa.q: What did Bilal start doing every morning at six?
qa.a: Coming to the gym and running hill sprints alone.

qa.q: Why might training so hard feel like relief to Bilal?
qa.a: It gives his anger about his father leaving a job to do, so he can feel strong instead of helpless.

qa.q: What choice did Marek make after Thursday's session, and why?
qa.a: He praised the effort but named its limits, offering sleep, the club counsellor or himself, because the anger underneath still needs attention.

qa.q: How might Bilal's teammates see the change from slamming lockers to hill sprints?
qa.a: They may be relieved he is less explosive, without noticing the limp or skipped meals that worried Marek.

grounding: A rugby coach in Poland sees a young player turn anger about his father leaving into relentless training, and urges rest and talking as well.

The university athletics track opened at five, and for three weeks Raghav had been there when the gates unlocked. Coach Vidya noted it in her log. After his public row with the hostel warden he had been benched for a meet, and he'd come back different: silent, running intervals until he retched, refusing the cool-down. His times were improving faster than anyone's.
On Friday she called him into the small office beside the equipment room. "This is the best you've trained all year," she said. "And I'm worried. Anger makes good fuel, but it burns the engine if you never stop. I want two rest days a week, and I want you to talk to someone about the warden business: me, the student counsellor, or a friend."
Raghav crossed his arms. "I'm fine."
"Then resting will be easy," Vidya said, and wrote it on his schedule.

qa.a: At five.

passage:
Dear Thomas,
I'm writing this instead of saying it after practice, because you'd nod and run off to do more sprints.
Since your suspension in August for that red card, you've changed. You're at the ground before me, you stay after the lights go off, and you've cut six seconds off your fitness-test time. I can see where the anger went, and honestly, it's a better place than the referee's face.
But I've also noticed you haven't missed a single session, even with your hamstring tight. You skip the team dinners. When Joel asked about your family last week, you went straight back to the cones.
Training this hard is only healthy if you also rest, and if someone knows what's underneath. So: two rest days a week, starting now, no arguments. My door is open on Thursdays, or there's the college counsellor. You choose.
Coach Noor

qa.q: Why was Thomas suspended in August?
qa.a: For that red card.

qa.q: What does Coach Noor believe Thomas's relentless training is really about?
qa.a: Coach Noor sees it as anger being redirected: the energy that once went at the referee now goes into sprints and extra sessions.

qa.q: What did Coach Noor add to make the new channel healthy?
qa.a: Two rest days a week and an open door on Thursdays, or the college counsellor, so Thomas both rests and has someone to talk to about what's underneath.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel reading "no arguments" from Coach Noor?
qa.a: Thomas may be frustrated at first, since training has become the way to cope, but may also feel seen and cared for beyond the stopwatch.

grounding: Shows a coach who sees a volatile player pour anger into relentless training and warns that it stays healthy only with rest and talking about what lies underneath.

The court lights at our college in Kochi go off at eight now. I made sure of that last season, because of Karthik. I'm Sabina, and I've coached volleyball here for six years.
Karthik had a rough year off court: his parents were splitting up, and he'd thrown a ball at the referee's stand and sat out two matches. Then something switched. He was at the court before sunrise, doing wall sets until his fingers were raw. He barely spoke. His game went through the roof.
Part of me was thrilled. Every coach wants that hunger. But I'd seen this before, and I didn't want to cheer it blindly. One evening I switched the lights off and sat him down on the bench. "This drive is good. It only stays good if you sleep, take Sundays off, and talk to someone about home. Me, or the counsellor."
He glared. Then he said, "Maybe the counsellor." That was the real win of the season.

qa.q: What was Karthik doing before sunrise?
qa.a: He was at the court, doing wall sets until his fingers were raw.

qa.q: Why didn't Sabina simply cheer Karthik's new hunger?
qa.a: Sabina had seen this before and suspected the anger about home was driving the training, which could wear him down if he never rested or talked.

qa.q: Which choice by Sabina made the season's "real win" possible?
qa.a: Switching the lights off and naming the conditions, sleep, Sundays off and talking to someone, while still praising the drive.

qa.q: What would change if Karthik kept training without rest or talking?
qa.a: He might keep improving for a while but could burn out or get hurt, and the pain about his parents would still be there, just buried under training.

grounding: Illustrates a coach who spots a volatile player turning anger into relentless training and insists the channel needs rest and talking about home to stay healthy.

passage: I'm Lavanya, assistant coach of the university hockey team in Ranchi, and this is what I saw with Anand this term. I don't know everything going on inside him. After his parents separated in January, he got angry a lot: snapping at teammates, kicking the bench. Then he changed. He started coming to practice an hour early and leaving an hour late. Sprints, drills, drag-flicks, again and again. His game got much better. Everyone was impressed. But I noticed he'd stopped sitting with the team at lunch. He looked exhausted. He trained on the rest day, alone. So one evening I sat with him on the bench. I said, "Your training's amazing. And I've noticed you never rest now, or talk about how you're doing. Both matter." He didn't reply for a long time. Then he asked if the team counsellor was any good.

September: Indu, the volleyball coach, watched Jeevan throw the ball at the wall after a lost match and storm off. He'd been angry all season.
October: Jeevan changed. He trained twice a day, spiking until his palm was red, lifting weights before class. His game became powerful. The team called him the machine.
November: Indu noticed he'd lost weight, came in with dark circles, and hadn't laughed in weeks. After practice she called him over. "You've turned all that anger into brilliant work. I'm proud of that. But machines break without rest. Are you sleeping? Is there something under this you want to talk about?" Jeevan looked at the floor. "My brother's sick," he said quietly. Indu nodded. "Then take Sunday off. And let's talk to the counsellor together on Monday."

qa.a: The machine.

qa.q: Why did Indu speak to Jeevan in November?
qa.a: Indu felt worried seeing his weight loss, dark circles and no laughter, signs the channel had become unhealthy without rest or talking.

qa.q: What did Indu suggest, and why is it a good balance?
qa.a: Taking Sunday off and talking to the counsellor together, so he keeps the healthy outlet but also rests and faces what's underneath.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel after saying his brother is sick?
qa.a: Jeevan might feel exposed but relieved to finally share what's been driving him.

grounding: Shows a coach seeing a volatile player turn anger into relentless training and cautioning that it is healthy only with rest and talking.

passage: Kalyani, you're coaching now, so let me, Nikita, tell you about a player I nearly lost. I was twenty-six, coaching the girls' football team at the college in Shillong. We had a forward, Rina, twenty, with a fierce temper. She'd been shouting at referees all year. Then, suddenly, she channelled it all into training. Six days a week, extra sessions, she never missed. Her shooting became lethal. I was delighted; I thought the problem was solved. But one day she fainted during warm-up. She hadn't slept properly in weeks, and she'd been skipping meals to train more. That's when I learnt: turning anger into effort is good, but only if the player sleeps, eats, and has someone to tell what's driving it. After that, I made Rina take rest days, and I sat with her every Friday to ask how she really was.

qa.a: Rina fainting in warm-up; after that, Nikita made Rina take rest days and talked with her every Friday.

qa.a: Rina might have felt awkward at first but also cared for, since someone noticed more than her goals.

The floodlights at the district ground had failed, the monsoon had turned the outfield to mud, and Suraj was still running shuttles at nine at night in the one pool of light from the pavilion.

Coach Hemant watched from under the tin roof. Since Suraj had been dropped from the state squad after a shouting match with a selector, he'd been first in and last out every day. He bowled until his fingers split. He skipped the team dinner twice.

It was better than the shouting. Hemant knew that. But he also saw how Suraj's jaw stayed clenched even after a good spell.

He walked out into the drizzle. "Enough for tonight."
"One more set."
"No. This fire is useful, Suraj. But tomorrow is rest. And on Friday, before nets, you and I sit and talk about the selector. Properly."
Suraj stared at the mud, then nodded.

qa.q: Where was Suraj running shuttles?
qa.a: Suraj was running shuttles in the one pool of light from the pavilion.

qa.q: What was Coach Hemant feeling as he watched Suraj train?
qa.a: Coach Hemant felt relieved the anger had gone into training instead of shouting, but uneasy about the clenched jaw and the missed dinners.

qa.q: What caution did the coach give, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The coach called the fire useful but ordered rest and a real talk about the selector, because training alone can't settle what is underneath.

qa.q: What is it like for Suraj to be told "Enough for tonight"?
qa.a: Suraj probably feels frustrated at first, wanting one more set, but also seen, since the coach names the selector without scolding.

grounding: Shows a coach who sees a dropped player pour anger into endless training and insists on rest and a real talk as well.

At the Andheri turf, Kunal had coached for six years and seen all kinds of players. Rafiq was new: fast, fierce, and in March he had kicked a bench so hard it cracked, after an argument at home he wouldn't explain.

Now, three months later, Rafiq was first to arrive and last to leave. Extra sprints, extra shooting drills, extra gym in the mornings. His touch had sharpened beautifully. Kunal was glad; this was a much better place for the anger than a bench.

But Kunal also saw the dark circles, the way Rafiq flinched when a teammate asked about his family, and the Sunday he trained on a swollen ankle.

After practice Kunal handed him water. "You've found a good outlet. Keep it. But an outlet with no rest breaks too. Take Sunday off. And if the home stuff gets heavy, I'm around, or we find you someone to talk to." Rafiq looked away, then nodded.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do to a bench in March?
qa.a: Rafiq kicked a bench so hard it cracked.

qa.q: What did Kunal feel seeing Rafiq's extra training?
qa.a: Kunal felt glad the anger had a better place than a bench, but worried by the dark circles, the flinch and the swollen ankle.

qa.q: Why is Kunal's advice about Sunday and talking wise?
qa.a: It keeps the healthy channel while guarding against burnout, and opens a door to talk about the trouble at home underneath.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel when Kunal mentions the home stuff?
qa.a: Rafiq may feel uncomfortable and exposed, but also quietly relieved that someone noticed and is offering help.

"Ojas, that's your fourth hour today."
"I'm fine, Coach. Just serves."
"You've served a hundred and twenty. I counted."
"Good, then I'm getting better." Thwack.
"You are. Your serve's the best on the team since the tournament." Himani caught the next ball and held it. "The tournament where you threw the chair."
Ojas wiped his face. "I said sorry for that."
"You did. And this," she spun the ball, "is a far better place for that anger than a chair. I mean it."
"So let me train."
"Train, yes. But you haven't taken a rest day in three weeks, and you still haven't told anyone what made you throw it. The court helps. It doesn't replace sleeping. Or talking."
A long silence. "It was my dad. On the phone. Before the match."
"Okay," Himani said, setting the ball down. "Sit. Tell me."

passage:
Wednesday night.
Sahil ran the stadium stairs forty times after practice today. Alone, in the rain. Since his brother's accident, he has gone from the angriest player on my team, the one who threw his racket, to the most driven. The others are impressed. I was too, at first. But I watched his face on the stairs, and it wasn't joy. It looked like punishment. Tomorrow I'm going to tell him how proud I am of the work, and also that the channel is only healthy if he rests and talks. I'll ask whether he has spoken to anyone about his brother. And I'll keep him off the stairs on Sunday, whatever he says.
Elizabeth
